clinician.final_diagnosis: Splenic infarction secondary to paroxysmal atrial fibrillation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old female with colonic Crohn's disease status post colectomy with Hartman's pouch ileostomy (3 weeks prior) presented to the ED with persistent nausea, abdominal pain (onset 2-3 days post-procedure), high ostomy output, generalized weakness, decreased oral intake, and reduced urine output. Physical examination revealed mild distress, generalized abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs, and a patent ileostomy with regular heart rate and rhythm. Laboratory studies on admission showed severe acute kidney injury (creatinine 9.56, baseline 0.56), hyponatremia (sodium 124), metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate 9), thrombocytosis (platelets 493), and severe acidemia (pH 7.13). CT imaging with contrast demonstrated multiple splenic infarctions of the entire lower pole with occlusion of branch splenic arteries. During hospitalization, telemetry monitoring documented a paroxysmal atrial fibrillation episode with spontaneous reversion to sinus rhythm within one day; the patient was asymptomatic during the AFib episode. Echocardiography revealed normal left ventricular ejection fraction without vegetation or patent foramen ovale. Thrombophilia workup (phospholipid antibodies and JAK2 mutation testing) was negative, ruling out alternative thrombotic etiologies. Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was determined to be the embolic source of the splenic infarction. The patient was discharged on apixaban (anticoagulation) and metoprolol (rate control).

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation documented on telemetry during hospitalization
Normal cardiac structure and function on echocardiography, ruling out structural sources of embolism
Thrombophilia workup negative, supporting AFib as the embolic source rather than hypercoagulable state
Clinical presentation consistent with acute splenic infarction: abdominal pain, nausea, weakness, and severe metabolic derangement
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation identified as the culprit of splenic infarction and patient treated with anticoagulation and rate control
